title: Comparative Analysis of the Tissue Quality of Surgical Scars and Healthy Tissue, and How It Is Influenced by Individual Local Osteopathic Treatment: A Randomized Controlled Trial
summary:
Background & Objective: Surgical scars can be visually unappealing, but they can also cause pain, restrict movement, or feel numb. Initial studies show that gentle hands-on treatments, such as osteopathy, can relieve these complaints. Since there is currently a lack of reliable data, this study examines the exact differences between scar tissue and healthy skin, and tests whether a targeted hands-on treatment can improve the quality of the scar.

Method: A total of 109 people with surgical scars are participating in this study. Participants are randomly divided into two groups. The first group receives a special, hands-on osteopathic treatment for the scar. The second group receives a sham treatment that feels similar but has no targeted medical effect. This is necessary to accurately compare the real effects. Skin firmness and the mobility of the tissue under the skin are examined painlessly using a small pressure-measuring device (MyotonPRO) and ultrasound. Pain sensitivity is assessed using a pressure pulse measuring device to determine the pain threshold, combined with thermal imaging to examine the temperature of the scar tissue.

Expected Results & Relevance: It is suspected that the scar tissue is firmer and less mobile compared to the healthy side of the body, and that the osteopathic treatment noticeably improves these properties. Following treatment, the scar tissue is less sensitive to pain and its temperature has equalised with that of the surrounding tissue. The results of the study are intended to help improve the treatment of surgical scars for everyone affected in the future and to provide scientific evidence of how effective osteopathic treatments are.

interventions.name: Combined, local osteopathic scar treatment according to Guillaume (2009) and Liedler (2020) (3 sessions of 20 minutes each over 3 weeks)
Control group receiving standardised sham treatment (3 sessions of 20 minutes each over 3 weeks)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Existing surgical scar (at least 6 months old, no more than 20 years old and still visible)
Scar length between 2 cm and 20 cm
Unilateral scar (the contralateral side serves as a reference)
Exclusion criteria:
other treatment of the scar during the study period
suffering from an autoimmune skin condition (atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, etc.)
or acute conditions requiring treatment (infectious diseases, tumours)
or connective tissue disorders
or a current pregnancy
